Plan this as a Rhylthyme protocol and deliver a live timeline: Passaging Two Flasks of Adherent HEK293 Cells for two T75 flasks split 1:6 into four, following the source text below
Resource limits: one biosafety cabinet, one 37 °C water bath, one CO₂ incubator, one benchtop centrifuge, one microscope with haemocytometer, one operator.
Steps:
1. Check the public catalog first (search_public_recipes or run_protocol). If a good match exists, use it and stop — its result already has the live URL.
2. Otherwise read rhylthyme://guide/authoring and build a program: one track per parallel line of work, sequential steps chained with afterStep, realistic durations, and a resourceConstraint for every task.
3. Express the limits as constraints, not as copied JSON. A machine that runs one job at a time is `resourceConstraints[].maxConcurrent`. Work repeated n times (n trays, n samples, n aircraft) is `replicates: {count: n, mode: "serial" | "parallel" | "stagger"}` on ONE step — never n hand-copied steps or tracks. Chain what follows each repetition with `{"type":"afterStep","stepId":"<step>","instances":"each"}`, and give the step that waits for all of them `"instances":"all"`. When a holding area between them only fits k at a time (a rack that holds two trays, a rotor that holds six tubes, a taxiway that holds two aircraft), set `replicates.maxInFlight: k` so the upstream step is held back instead of stranding the downstream one.
4. Run validate_program and fix every error it reports.
5. Run analyze_schedule to check the makespan, critical path and resource conflicts; adjust offsets so tracks finish together. Its `bindingConstraints` say which limit is actually gating the makespan.
6. Call visualize_schedule and give the user the live URL plus the Gantt/itinerary from the result. Do not describe the schedule in prose.

Source text to schedule (read all of it):
<<<
Passaging Two Flasks of Adherent HEK293 Cells

Two T75 flasks at about 90 % confluence are split 1:6 into four new flasks. The room has one biosafety cabinet, one 37 °C water bath, one CO₂ incubator, one benchtop centrifuge and one microscope with a haemocytometer. Only one flask can be open in the cabinet at a time, so the two flasks queue for it while the centrifuge and the microscope stay free. Work with pre-warmed medium, PBS and trypsin-EDTA throughout; nothing cold touches the cells. One operator.

Preparation
1. Wipe down the cabinet, lay out pipettes and tubes, and let the blower run; 10 minutes.
2. Check both flasks on the microscope for confluence and contamination; 10 minutes.

Flask A
3. Aspirate the spent medium and rinse the monolayer with 5 mL of PBS; 4 minutes in the cabinet.
4. Add 2 mL of trypsin-EDTA, rock the flask and return it to the incubator for 5 minutes.
5. Knock the flask, check detachment and neutralise with 8 mL of medium; 5 minutes in the cabinet.
6. Transfer the suspension to a 15 mL tube and spin at 300 × g for 5 minutes.
7. Aspirate the supernatant and resuspend the pellet in 10 mL of fresh medium; 4 minutes.
8. Count the cells on the haemocytometer; 6 minutes.
9. Seed two new T75 flasks at 1:6 and label them; 6 minutes in the cabinet.
10. Return the new flasks to the incubator and leave them to settle overnight, at least 16 hours.

Flask B
11. Start flask B the moment flask A leaves the cabinet: aspirate and rinse with 5 mL of PBS; 4 minutes.
12. Trypsinise flask B in the incubator for 5 minutes.
13. Neutralise flask B as soon as flask A is out of the cabinet again; 5 minutes.
14. Spin flask B at 300 × g for 5 minutes once the centrifuge is free.
15. Resuspend the flask B pellet in 10 mL of fresh medium; 4 minutes.
16. Count flask B on the haemocytometer once flask A has been counted; 6 minutes.
17. Seed two more T75 flasks at 1:6 and label them; 6 minutes.
18. Return them to the incubator to settle overnight alongside the first pair.

Finishing
19. Wipe the cabinet down, discard the waste and switch the blower to standby; 10 minutes.
20. Write the passage number, the split ratio and the counts into the culture log; 5 minutes.
>>>

Looking at the source text, I modeled the two flasks as a single **replicated chain** (count = 2) that runs through the shared bottleneck resources (cabinet, incubator, centrifuge, microscope), exactly like the "three trays, one oven" pattern — no copy‑pasted per‑flask steps. The cabinet's `maxConcurrent: 1` reproduces "only one flask open in the cabinet at a time" and naturally staggers Flask B behind Flask A at every cabinet/centrifuge/microscope step, while the incubator (`maxConcurrent: 2`) lets both flasks' unattended incubation steps run concurrently, freeing the cabinet for the other flask — matching "start flask B the moment flask A leaves the cabinet."
